articles.title: Spain sees widespread disruption in first general strike for 14 years
articles.summary: Protests are also expected in the biggest cities less than three weeks before Spaniards vote in parliamentary elections.
body: The general strike took place little more than two weeks ahead of national elections in Spain
Transport and other public services across Spain have faced serious disruption in the first general strike for 14 years called by the main unions over housing and the high cost of living.
Demonstrations were also planned later on Wednesday, with the biggest protests expected in Madrid and Barcelona. Spaniards are due to vote in parliamentary elections on 29 November.
The head of the big UGT labour union, Pepe Álvarez, said the strike was a success with "massive" participation, while Unai Sordo of the CC OO union said turnout was "very significant."
However, the Spanish Confederation of Business Organisations said participation was "low and uneven", depending on the areas and sectors involved.
Some of the biggest disruption on Wednesday was seen in the main industrial hubs of Madrid and the north-eastern region of Catalonia where traffic was halted on several main roads.
The interior ministry said dozens of people were arrested for a variety of incidents and Spanish reports said estate agencies had seen attacks on their offices.

The strike was triggered by widespread protests over affordable housing and rising living costs, after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from a flat in Madrid where she had lived for seven decades. She died in hospital weeks later.

Rental prices in the capital have soared in recent years. The monthly cost of a 50m sq apartment in Madrid was an average of €1,170 in October, according to property portal Idealista, while Spain's average gross monthly salary is about €2,460 (£2,056).
That amounts to nearly half the average gross salary, well above the 30% level of affordability often recommended by housing experts and public institutions.
Tyres were on fire in the city of Gijon in northern Spain
Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called snap elections last month after parliament failed to approve his plan for housing reform.
Not since 2012, under the conservative government of Mariano Rajoy, has Spain held general strikes.

And while previous strikes have been problematic for the government in power, this one is different. Sánchez and his ministers have even encouraged workers to down tools and demand affordable housing.
"Your eight-hour day. Your pension. Your public healthcare… These were collective conquests," he wrote on social media, praising those who took part in previous strikes.
Dramatic eviction of woman aged 87 highlights Spain's housing shortage
Spanish PM Sánchez calls early election after housing protests
The conservative People's Party (PP), by contrast, has accused the government of attempting to weaponise the strike for electoral gain.

PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo called the general strike "nonsense", calling the unions "mafia" and "trash". Feijoo's party is leading in the polls and party spokesman Miguel Tellado accused the government of exploiting the strike to warn voters against allowing a right-wing government to be formed, which looks the most likely outcome of the 29 November election.
Sánchez told Spanish TV this week: "What is nonsense is to question the rights of workers to strike."
Gonzalo Álvarez, who was taking part in the general strike, says 50% of his salary goes towards rent
Among those taking part in the general strike was Gonzalo Álvarez, 27, who was visiting different picket lines in central Madrid.
Although he works in sales, he has been volunteering for a housing union that tries to protect tenants and makes them aware of their rights.
The eviction of Maricarmen Abascal at the end of September "was the little fire" that sparked this protest, he told the BBC.
Álvarez knew the 87-year-old, who had faced a tripling of her rent under new landlords, and says he was deeply upset by her treatment.

He rents a small, one-bedroom flat with his girlfriend, a dental hygienist, in the city's southern Arganzuela disrict. The couple pay €1,000 between them, which means each spends about half of their salary on housing, even before other bills.
"It's absolutely crazy… with the food, with the electricity, with the water, with gas."
He sees no way of getting on the property ladder: "You have to collect an insane amount of money to be able to buy a house. So with these salaries, it's impossible."
With current rent and purchase prices, he believes buying somewhere is "completely impossible".
However, the vice-president of the CEOE, Spanish biggest business association, Miguel Garrido, criticised the strike, complaining that businesses had little to do with the price of housing.
"This is not a strike for labour-related reasons, but rather for political ones, and it is closely linked to the early calling of elections," he said.
Demonstrations were planned for some of Spain's biggest cities later in the day and the scale of support will be widely viewed as an indicator of public discontent ahead of the election.
Another reliable indicator of support for strikes is the level of demand for electricity with Spain's industrial sector.

Power usage in Spain fell by 7.5% during the early hours of Wednesday, according to data from operator Red Eléctrica. During the last general strike 14 years ago, equivalent consumption was down by more than 15%.
Police detained a protester in Madrid during the general strike

articles.title: Australian teen missing in bush for six days rescued alive
articles.summary: The 17-year-old's mum has joked that he is "grounded for life" and "never leaving the house again".
body: A teenager missing for six days in dense Australian bushland has been found alive.
William, whose surname has not been released, disappeared last Friday while on a camping trip with a friend in bushland about 180km (112 miles) east of Melbourne, Victoria.
Extremely cold overnight temperatures had left authorities concerned for the 17-year-old's welfare. Police dogs, divers and helicopters had been involved in the search.
He was located on Friday morning and reunited with his relieved family, who said he was uninjured but "grounded for life".
Rescuers winched William to safety, and fed him a doughnut and a bottle of water, before he was taken to hospital for a check up.
The boy's mother, Elizabeth Barkley, told reporters the teenager had "only a few scratches" and seemed fit and healthy.
"He's doing fine, everything seems to be fine, he's in perfect health," she added.
"He just stayed in one spot and waited to be rescued and I'm just over the moon he's alive."
Joking, she added: "He's never leaving the house again."
Police have said officers were emotional to have found the teen alive.
"It doesn't happen all the time," Victoria Police Acting Inspector Jason Benbow said. "I'm sure he's got a story to tell us soon, which we're very keen to hear," he added.

articles.title: Indonesia's vice president resigns amid signs ruling alliance is fraying
articles.summary: The news comes at a turbulent time for Prabowo, who faces a growing rift with his predecessor Joko Widodo.
body: Gibran Rakabuming Raka has been mired in a growing controversy over his high school credentials

Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has submitted his resignation, an aide has told the BBC, in a move which could further strain the political alliance that helped propel President Prabowo Subianto to power.
It comes after Indonesia's Supreme Court ruled that a high-school document used during Gibran's 2024 election campaign was invalid.
The ruling prompted more than 100 lawmakers to support a parliamentary initiative that could have paved the way for proceedings to impeach Gibran.
The aide, Budi Arie, said Gibran's resignation letter was submitted directly to Prabowo on Wednesday. It remains unclear if it has been accepted.
Gibran has long faced controversy over whether his high school qualifications met legal requirements to run for office.
Having studied in Singapore and Australia, he had used an Indonesian equivalence certificate to demonstrate his educational credentials.
Indonesian law requires vice-presidents to have completed senior secondary school or its equivalent, but the Supreme Court found no evidence to prove Gibran had graduated.
"No evidence was found to show Gibran had a foreign diploma or certificate that could serve as the basis for equivalency with a senior high school or equivalent qualification," it said.
It also considered a Constitutional Court ruling from earlier in October which came to the same conclusion.
Gibran previously argued that undertaking university education was sufficient proof that he had completed senior high school.
On Tuesday, he asked for the chance to challenge the ruling and be given the opportunity to prove the legitimacy of his education credentials, State Secretary Prasetyo Hadi said.

Gibran's ascension to Prabowo's ticket in the 2024 election was part of an alliance formed between his father, outgoing president Joko Widodo - known as Jokowi - and Prabowo, his erstwhile bitter rival.
Gibran was 36 at the time, and only became eligible for candidacy after a controversial ruling by the Constitutional Court, which exempted him from the minimum age requirement of 40.
His resignation comes as tensions between Jokowi and Prabowo appear to have flared.

Since taking the presidency, Prabowo has shown little interest in pushing ahead with Jokowi's legacy project: the construction of Nusantara, a new capital. Instead, he has focused much of the state's resources on his own flagship programme to provide free school meals across the country.
In a series of personnel reshuffles over the past year, Prabowo has also shifted many Jokowi loyalists into new roles, including long-serving finance minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati.
Last week, authorities arrested presidential chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo - no relation - on suspicions of wiretapping the president.

Prabowo sacked Listyo a day later, in what many pointed to as a sign of a crumbling alliance: Listyo, who formerly served as the national police chief, is widely considered a long-time ally of Jokowi.

Within the government, allegiances seem to be shifting. On Monday, three members of Prabowo's cabinet collectively resigned from the party led by Kaesang Pangarep, Jokowi's youngest son, citing their desire to focus on their duties in Prabowo's administration.

All this is unfolding at a particularly turbulent period in Prabowo's presidency. The free school meals programme is struggling for funding, parts of Indonesia have recently battled the country's worst wildfires in a decade, and the national stock market faces crisis amid allegations of widespread market manipulation.
On Tuesday, students across the country staged demonstrations to protest against the government's handling of a range of issues, including the environmental crisis and corruption.

articles.title: Famed ship SS United States to be sunk off coast of Florida
articles.summary: Activists unsuccessfully fought for the historic liner to be preserved and turned into a museum, but it will now become the world's largest artificial ocean reef.
body: This archival video shows the SS United States in 2025 as it starts its move to Florida on its way to become the world's largest artificial reef.
A ship that was once the fastest in the world and is longer than the Titanic will be sunk off the coast of Florida and turned into the world's largest artificial ocean reef.
The SS United States spent nearly 30 years docked in Philadelphia before it was moved to Florida, where it will soon become a home for sealife and an underwater attraction for marine enthusiasts.
Activists unsuccessfully fought for the historic liner - which crossed the Atlantic Ocean hundreds of times - to be preserved as a museum.
Instead, after being purchased by a Florida county, it will be added to the dozens of artificial reefs off the coast, as a land-based museum detailing the ship's history is also planned.
Before its retirement, the SS United States was known for carrying royalty and celebrities from the US the Europe, beginning in 1952 and ending in 1969.
A young Bill Clinton, before he was president, used the ship to cross the Atlantic. Former presidents Harry Truman, Dwight Eisenhower and John Kennedy also travelled on the vessel.

The ship was moved from Philadelphia to Alabama last year for cleaning and remediation work. On Monday, it took its final journey from Alabama to the coast of Destin, Florida, where it will be sunk on Wednesday in a precision operation without explosives.
A 2015 image from when the ship was docked in Philadelphia
Stars including Marlon Brando, Coco Chanel, Duke Ellington, Salvador Dali, Walt Disney, Judy Garland and Cary Grant also boarded the ship during its sailing lifetime.
Before its purchase by the municipal Florida government, a number of proposals that would have seen the ship live a second life as a museum or a floating hotel failed.
Instead, the famed ship sat at various docks with various owners as legal battles played out.
The SS United States Conservancy group repeatedly attempted to keep the ship above water, but was unsuccessful.
Conservancy President Susan Gibbs - whose grandfather helped design the SS United States - said she was glad that the story of the ship would live on.
"[The ship] has always been this unabashedly American symbol that brings so many people together," Gibbs told CBS News, the BBC's US partner.

articles.title: Kidnapper, 74, escapes from house arrest in Argentina by abseiling from balcony
articles.summary: Leonardo Bertulazzi, a former member of the Marxist guerrilla group the Red Brigades, was about to be extradited to his home country of Italy.
body: Leonardo Bertulazzi was first arrested in Buenos Aires in 2002
A 74-year-old Italian man who was found guilty of a kidnapping carried out by a far-left militant group in the 1970s has escaped while under house arrest in Argentina and is on the run.
Leonardo Bertulazzi used a harness to abseil down from a fifth-floor balcony in the capital, Buenos Aires.

His escape was not immediately registered because he had tampered with his electronic ankle monitor so that it continued to transmit body temperature measurements even after he had prised it open and absconded.
Bertulazzi already spent decades as a fugitive after he was sentenced in absentia in Italy for the 1977 kidnapping of Italian naval engineer Pietro Costa.
He was awaiting extradition to Italy and was being monitored by the Argentine ministry of security through an ankle tag which registers the wearer's body temperature and movements.
Officials said that they had become suspicious when they noticed that the tag had remained stationary.
When they entered the fifth-floor apartment in the centre of Buenos Aires, Bertulazzi was gone, but the ankle monitor remained.

Wary of Bertulazzi's past with the Marxist guerilla group the Red Brigades and his bomb-making skills, police called in explosives experts in case it had been rigged to detonate, according to Argentine newspaper Clarín.
However, the experts found that while Bertulazzi had tampered with the device, he had done so to prevent the alarm from sounding once he removed it.
A nationwide manhunt is now under way.
Italian media say that his extradition to Italy had been imminent after his last appeal was rejected.
Bertulazzi was first arrested after using a false passport to cross into Argentina from neighbouring Chile in 2002.
However, he was granted refugee status in 2004 and lived freely in the South American country until his re-arrest in 2024, when the current right-wing president, Javier Milei, took office.
Milei's government said at the time that "Bertulazzi is responsible for crimes that undermined democratic values and the lives of many victims".
He was a member of the Red Brigades, which kidnapped and killed a number of state officials in the 1970s and '80s.
Bertulazzi was part of the Red Brigades' Genoa section that kidnapped Pietro Costa on the street and then held him for 81 days before receiving a big ransom.

The money it made from the kidnapping was then used to buy a flat in Rome, which was used in 1978 for the Red Brigades' most notorious crime, the kidnap and murder of Italian former Prime Minister, Aldo Moro.

Moro was abducted when his car was ambushed on the way to the opening of parliament. He was held in the flat for 54 days before he was shot and his body abandoned in the boot of a Renault car in the centre of Rome.

articles.title: Six thousand Italian schools hit by threats in suspected bomb hoax
articles.summary: Emails containing the false warnings were sent to schools in Rome, Naples, Vicenza, Florence, Pisa, Trieste and other Italian cities, officials say.
body: These children had to leave their primary school in Rome as a result of one of the threats sent on Wednesday

Some 6,300 schools across Italy have received bomb threats, according to government in Rome, and Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara has said the incidents are probably a "cyber-attack, not a genuine risk".
Valditara told Italian TV that there was a clear strategy behind the rash of threats in Italy and elsewhere in Europe which had targeted flights, supermarkets and even hospitals.
The emails were sent to schools in Rome, Naples, Milan, Genoa, Vicenza, Florence, Pisa, Trieste and many other Italian cities, and a number of buildings were evacuated as a precaution.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni summoned top ministers and intelligence chiefs, while opposition leaders were due to meet her on Thursday.
Meloni said the government was monitoring closely the "numerous reports of bomb threats at educational institutions" although checks so far had not indicated any evidence of "concrete danger".
"These reports appear rather linked to a strategy intended to cause alarm and concern," she said on Facebook.

Italian airports along with airlines elsewhere in Europe were hit by a series of bomb hoaxes last week that prompted a series of scares, evacuations and widespread disruption. Although a number of threats were claimed by an extremist misogynistic group, it later denied any link to the false warnings.
Italian officials said a single email appeared to have been sent on Wednesday to the inboxes of 6,300 out of a total of 7,476 state schools, and private schools were unaffected.
The message, said to be from a certain "Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan", caused alarm in many schools.
One Milan headteacher, Anna Bertato, told Italian media she had checked the email address of the sender online: "It was already classified as spam by a student at a university in Taiwan."

Another Milan headteacher, Massimo Nunzio Barrella, told Adnkronos news agency that he had immediately realised the email was spam when it arrived in his inbox at 08:59 and he decided not to evacuate his school and reassured parents who phoned in.
"The text seemed almost comical," said Barrella, "it was like a message from Martians: 'We have come to annihilate you.' I even had a bit of a laugh."

Although many schools were initially evacuated on Wednesday, the alarm was quickly lifted, and pupils were allowed to return to class. Some parents decided to take their children home for the day, but the majority of schools in Milan did not send their pupils home.
Some 280 school head teachers had already received threats in recent days, according to Italian reports.

In a statement, the head of the central Umbria region Stefania Proietti said "checks conducted so far in Umbrian schools have proved negative, and law enforcement is working rapidly and carefully to verify each report".

In a separate incident, more than 300 schools in Northern Ireland were sent emails which police said they were treating as a hoax. Messages sent to number of schools in Scotland were also being treated by police as a hoax. It is unclear whether any of the incidents are connected.

articles.title: Missing 11-month-old baby found buried alive in a crate in South Carolina
articles.summary: Officials say the child was found close to his father's home on Tuesday, a day after he was taken, and is being cared for in hospital.
body: Watch: County Sheriff describes how buried baby was found
An 11-month-old baby has been rescued in South Carolina after officials say he was buried alive in a crate by his father.

Koah Sharpe had been missing since Monday when he was taken by his father, Michael Comer, 25, according to the Lexington County Sheriff's Department. Comer was arrested on a burglary charge on Monday evening but his son was not with him.

The baby was found on Tuesday "buried alive" and "clinging to life" not far from his father's house, Lexington County Sheriff Jay Koon said at a news conference. It is thought he had been there for 24 hours.
The child is now in hospital receiving care, Koon said, adding he was hopeful he would make a full recovery.
Police are still deciding what further charges to bring against the father.
The search for baby Koah began on Monday after his father took him from his mother's house.
Comer's mother was watching the child and had left her son alone with him briefly, Koon said, when he left abruptly with Koah.
Officials allege the baby's father buried him alive in a dog crate

Comer was seen travelling to multiple locations without the baby and was later arrested in Lexington County without Koah. A search party of 100 police and fire department officials were then sent to search for the child, the sheriff said.
He added that when they asked Comer where his son was, he "did not have much to say" about his whereabouts.

Koon said that rescuers searched the woods near Comer's house and saw some "freshly disturbed dirt". As they began to dig, they heard a baby crying - something the sheriff described as "the most joyful sound you ever heard".
"The race was on. Everybody was getting down there trying to get him out," Koon added.
He said the crate was wrapped in a towel that probably provided enough air for Koah to survive for as long as he did, while the cold weather kept him from getting too hot.

"The crate was, probably, I'm guessing about a two-foot [61cm] by two-foot dog crate. So, I think, once that crate hit the ground, he was probably up at least a foot from the top of that crate to the top of the ground," Koon explained.
Of the parents' relationship, the sheriff said there were "obviously some issues". Comer had previously pleaded guilty to domestic violence charges, court records show.

Comer's mother, Patricia Comer, told NBC News that Koah's mother had full custody of him but allowed her to supervise while her son watched him. She said her son had watched the baby before unsupervised without any problems.
"Honestly, I'm his mother, and I never expected this from him," Patricia Comer said.

articles.title: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent relocated after alleged Iranian threats
articles.summary: Bessent is now one of several Trump administration officials to live on military bases due to safety concerns.
body: The severity and nature of the threat against Scott Bessent remains unclear
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been moved from his Washington DC home to a military base after Iran-linked threats to his life, according to US media reports.
CBS, the BBC's US partner, said the relocation came after a photo of Bessent's home was published in the Wall Street Journal.
Bessent has been at the forefront of efforts to isolate Iran economically through sanctions and a wider economic blockade.
While the exact nature of the threats against Bessent remain unclear, US intelligence has warned that Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target Americans, including US officials.

"After the Wall Street Journal published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the secretary's Georgetown home to be geo-located, security concerns began to increase," a source told CBS.
Georgetown is an affluent part of Washington that is home to a number of government officials and prominent residents.
Those security concerns, the source added, prompted authorities to move Bessent to a military base in the area.
In a statement, a Treasury Department spokesperson said only that Bessent "will not be deterred" by threats and "remains committed" to the US effort to pressure Iran's economy.
The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.
In September, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned that Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target Americans.
The New York Times has reported that the Iranian effort includes the targeting of current and former US officials. One source told the newspaper this has "reached a more advanced stage".

Other US officials reportedly on Iran's list of potential targets include former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo, former National Security Advisor John Bolton and Mark Milley, the former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.
Milley and Bolton's security teams were taken away by the Trump administration shortly after he returned to office last year.

Bessent is one of a number of administration officials that live on military bases. The White House's new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, was moved to a base in late 2025 - before the conflict with Iran began.
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio both live on military bases, as did former Attorney General Pam Bondi and former intelligence chief Tulsi Gabbard.

The US and Israel launched an air campaign against Iran in February, killing its leader and prompting the regime in Tehran to retaliate with strikes on US allies across the region and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and gas usually travels.

In June, the US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated a blockade targeting Iranian ports.

articles.title: Four grizzly bears killed in Canada after fatal attack on mother and daughter
articles.summary: The sow and her three cubs were responsible for killing Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20, earlier this month.
body: Between 10,000 and 13,000 grizzly bears are estimated to live in British Columbia (file image)
Four grizzly bears have been killed in connection with a fatal attack on a mother and daughter in the Canadian province of British Columbia.
Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20, died earlier this month after going on an afternoon walk in a trail area in Bella Coola.
The British Columbia Conservation Office Service (BCCOS) launched an investigation into their deaths and forensic testing has since confirmed a sow and her three cubs were responsible for the attack.
All four were destroyed "in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines" to protect the public, BCCOS Inspector Jeff Tyre said in an update on Tuesday.
Mother and daughter die after suspected grizzly bear attack in Canada
"Evidence from the investigation as well as animal DNA was analysed and conclusively linked to a sow and its three offspring," he added.
The attack "likely involved predatory behaviour", which Tyre said was "very rare".
He added that more than a dozen conservation officers took part in the investigation over the past week, amid "difficult terrain and weather".
Balcarras and Reed were "two peas in a pod" who "got along really, really well" and shared many hobbies, Balcarras' brother, Josh, told CBC.
"When Jenny hiked, Selah was right there beside her," he said.
Tyre said DNA testing also confirmed the four bears were not involved in a 2025 attack on a school group also in the Bella Coola area.
The incident in November of last year saw 11 people injured, two of them critically, while the bear responsible was never found.

"Today, we have learned from the BC Conservation Officer Service members that they have captured and euthanized the bears involved in the recent fatal attack," said Samuel Schooner, Elected Chief of the Nuxalk Nation, in a statement.

"We would like to thank the BC Conservation Officer Service for their dedication and hard work to resolve this incident. This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year's attack. Our thoughts remain with the victims' families."

articles.title: Kenya discharges last Ebola patient in major milestone towards virus-free status
articles.summary: The country begins a 42-day countdown to being declared Ebola-free, provided no new cases are recorded.
body: Kenya has reported no new confirmed cases since 20 October 2026

Kenya has discharged its last Ebola patient - the seventh to recover from the virus - marking a major milestone in efforts to contain the disease in the East African nation, which now begins a 42-day countdown to officially being declared Ebola-free.
It had confirmed its first ever case of Ebola early in October when a Kenyan businessman died within days of arriving in the capital, Nairobi.
He had contracted the virus in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where more than 5,000 people have died in an ongoing outbreak that began in May. His mother also subsequently died.
Kenya's health minister said 135 identified contacts of the infected patients had also completed their 21 days in isolation.
"Today with the discharge of the last patient we can confirm and tell the world that seven patients have recovered - and all contacts have completed their follow-up monitoring," Aden Duale said.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) described it as an important achievement in the regional response to the outbreak.
"This is an encouraging moment for Kenya and for Africa. We must sustain surveillance and vigilance until the outbreak is officially declared over," Africa CDC chief Jean Kaseya posted on X.
What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult?
Kenya has reported no new confirmed cases since 20 October.
All the Kenyan cases were linked to the man who had travelled from DR Congo through Uganda, with health officials reporting no evidence of wider community transmission.
Those who have recovered following treatment included four healthcare workers.
Five patients were discharged on 3 November, followed by a sixth three days later, before the final patient was cleared on Wednesday.

Under World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines, 42 days must pass after the last patient tests negative and is discharged, or the last Ebola victim is safely buried, before an outbreak can be declared over.

The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit. The incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks.
Duale said the government would maintain heightened surveillance at border crossings, airports, health facilities and communities throughout the countdown.
Emergency response teams will remain on alert across the country, while the health authorities will continue monitoring travellers arriving from affected countries.

Kenyans returning from Ebola-affected areas are required to complete electronic health declarations before travelling, undergo screening on arrival and spend 21 days in quarantine under the supervision of health teams.
The minister also urged countries that had imposed travel and visa restrictions to reconsider them - adding that Kenya had no intention of serving as a quarantine centre for another country.
In May, a Kenyan court suspended US plans to open an Ebola quarantine facility for American citizens.
Kenya has maintained that there is no need to restrict domestic travel, trade or public gatherings.
The outbreak has nevertheless disrupted international travel, with some Gulf countries introducing restrictions affecting travellers from Kenya and other African countries.
Saudi Arabia stopped issuing visas to Kenyan nationals in late October, prompting concerns among those seeking employment there.
Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) has announced that it is lifting its suspension on issuing new visas to Ugandan nationals, easing restrictions introduced in June.
But Ugandans will have to spend at least 21 days outside of Uganda before being allowed to travel to the UAE.
The UAE is also allowing certain students, diplomatic passport holders and Ugandan embassy employees to enter under approved health procedures.
Uganda, which shares a long and busy border with DR Congo, was among the countries first affected but declared its own Ebola outbreak over on 27 August.
The current outbreak in DR Congo has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.

articles.title: The rise and fall of Jensen Huang - how the tech superstar became mired in scandal
articles.summary: Within days, Huang's status as a seemingly untouchable figure leading the global tech race has crumbled.
body: BBC's Samira Hussain reports from Wall Street on what the fall of the tech superstar means.

Jensen Huang, known for sporting a black leather jacket to shareholder events, appeared to have it all. He was courted by leaders in the US and China alike, worshipped by investors and seen as a loyal family man. But a rockstar approach to his personal life has ultimately led to his resignation.
The 63-year-old has been married since 1985, long before the foundation of Nvidia, the company that propelled him to tech stardom.

He is known as a workaholic and a demanding manager, with high standards for those who worked for him, which included his own children, promoted within the company. But he has seen his personal reputation go into freefall this week, undone by romantic entanglements that throw doubt on his focus and his judgement.

On Thursday, he resigned following back-to-back revelations of two affairs. News of the first - a relationship with a businesswoman alleged to be a Chinese spy - ricocheted around the world, raising eyebrows among investors. It was followed on Wednesday by reports that the tech boss had also had an affair with an Nvidia colleague.
His departure creates uncertainty in the global stock market, which was already knocked-off balance in recent weeks. Nvidia is a linchpin in the US's race for technology leadership with China.
Huang may not be a household name on the same level as Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg.

But his role in the tech industry, especially in relation to the explosion of artificial intelligence in the last three years, may prove more consequential. Nvidia dominates the market for the microchips that are used to power the new technology.
The company, which is still valued at nearly $4n (£3.02tn) despite recent events, is at the centre of the AI race between the US and China, the world's tech and economic powerhouses.
Huang enjoyed access to the seats of political power on an unrivalled scale, being courted by both US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping.

His remarkable rise to the top of his profession has led to him being dubbed the "Taylor Swift of tech" and seen him amass an estimated fortune of $145bn, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

Despite always donning his trademark all-black outfits and taking a playful approach to investor presentations, Huang has worked for years to present himself as a family man, someone who exemplified the American Dream.

Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang and his family moved to the west coast of the US when he was nine years old. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a Master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.
It was at college where he met his wife, Lori Mills. The pair were lab partners and married in 1985, eight years before Huang founded Nvidia.
They have two children, Madison and Spencer, who now both work in senior roles at Nvidia.

The company became a key provider of the computer chips and circuits used for gaming before it expanded in a new direction. It now creates the key processing chips used to power the growing AI technology.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns after tech giant rocked by second affair allegation
Who could replace Jensen Huang as Nvidia's chief executive?

Huang has hailed AI as a "new industrial revolution" that is on par with the advent of electricity. Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company and its customers include the biggest firms on the planet, Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, SpaceX, Tesla, OpenAI and Anthropic, all spending big on its products.

So it is no surprise that at a recent AI summit at the White House, Huang was picked out from a group of 42 to flank the president, alongside Elon Musk, both men with whom Trump has famously close relationships.

"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on Jensen Huang, told the BBC, referring to the late boss of Apple. He added that Huang was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.
He described him as a "demanding" boss, who "really pushes his people to the limit".
But while the former Nvidia CEO is "very brilliant" and a "world-class computer scientist", there's also "a level of arrogance" and "a level of self-deception as well", he said.
Huang had gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, he added, something that was "very important to him".

"He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways," Witt added. "The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family. But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad."

First reports emerged on 29 October in the New York Times that Huang had conducted a relationship with Alice Huang, no relation. US officials allege the businesswoman associated with Singapore-based firm Megaspeed is a Chinese intelligence asset.
After the revelations of the first affair, Huang admitted to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting their family.
Trump, as well as other leaders in the AI tech industry, initially backed Huang to continue in his role at Nvidia. The president described him as "honourable".

But the reporting of a second affair, with Kimberly Powell, vice president of healthcare who has worked at Nvidia for 18 years, prompted a board meeting, followed by the announcement Huang was stepping down.
In the aftermath of that news Trump said Huang had done "a fantastic job" and proposed Tim Cook of Apple as a suitable replacement at the head of Nvidia.

articles.title: Friday briefing: Why people are turning to folklore in our disconnected age
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: ​Old and new rituals still resonate in today’s folk revival which is being shaped by younger generations seeking spirituality, community and connection to nature
body: Good morning. What are your plans for this Friday 13th? Will you be edging your way through the day, alert to impending disasters and saluting every magpie you see (a cheerful “good day, captain” works for me). Or will you be powering past the superstition with the insouciance that accompanies the certainty this is, probably, just another day?

Either way, I’ve noticed that folklore – the rituals, traditions and stories we share together – is enjoying a significant revival across our pop culture and community practice, powered by the younger generation and accelerated by online connections.
This explosion in engagement is the opposite of dusty nostalgia but instead focused on very contemporary concerns about connection with both the Earth and each other.

For today’s newsletter, as a major survey charting contemporary folk culture in England comes to an end next month, I spoke to three folklore experts about why these customs still matter. First, this morning’s headlines.

Technology | Microsoft 365, Outlook, Teams and other apps were disrupted for thousands of users for more than nine hours, with Microsoft scrambling to find a solution after initial fixes failed to bring services back online.

US news | Nvidia’s ousted CEO Jensen Huang and Donald Trump’s commerce secretary are expected to testify before Congress in the coming weeks, as the fallout from Huang’s reported affair with an alleged Chinese spy sparked bipartisan concerns for national security and calls for a tougher stance against Beijing.

UK news | Young people with disabilities will lose their personal independence payments and will have to apply to a local fund for short-term expenses and equipment, Alan Milburn’s review will recommend.
UK politics | Nigel Farage appeared on Russell Brand’s US podcast nine months after the comedian was investigated by police over allegations of sexual assault, the Guardian has learned.
Climate crisis | China has ruled out hosting the Cop33 UN climate summit in 2028 after months of deliberations, leaving the field open for other Asian countries to hold it, the Guardian understands.

It’s been hard to miss the wave of representations of folkloric tales and practice in popular media in recent years – think folk horror movies like Hereditary, Midsommar and The Ritual on the big screen, or The League of Gentlemen, the Detectorists and Small Prophets on the small screen.

This has been accompanied by thriving online folk communities, many aimed at gen Z, exploring urban legends, spell-making and paganism, and offline a surge in people actively participating in seasonal calendar customs. ​There’s the Mari Lwyd local to south Wales, a ghastly skeletal hobby horse who travels around people’s houses in midwinter with a group of wassailers to scare and entertain, and Whuppity Scoorie, a children’s spring festival in Lanark, first documented in the 1890s. And with renewed interest comes an expanded community: Jack in the Green, the annual May Day skirmish in Hastings, has included a LGBTQI+ troupe for 30 years.

Folklorists tracking this revival wanted to learn more, resulting in the National Folklore Survey for England, coordinated by the Centre for Contemporary Legend at Sheffield Hallam University. An ambitious two-year undertaking, which draws to a close in December, it is based around a snapshot study of almost 2,000 participants and provides the most comprehensive picture of contemporary folk culture in England to date.

Dr Diane A Rodgers, the project co-lead, and researcher Dr Sophie Parkes-Nield are still collating their embarrassment of data, but some fascinating trends have already emerged. These include the prevalence of beliefs (one-third of respondents believe that ghosts exist) and that younger age-groups were twice as likely to believe in conspiracy theories, demons and curses as older respondents. There’s also the intergenerational reach of contemporary legends: nearly half of 16- to 24-year-olds believe that Diana, Princess of Wales was murdered as a result of a conspiracy, despite not being born when she died in 1997.
The results also reveal how folkloric practice is woven into everyday life. I’m not alone in my acknowledgment of magpies: 51% do something similar, whether that’s saluting, speaking or spitting.

“Do you say something when you see a magpie? Do you pick a penny off the pavement? Do you touch wood when you want something to happen?” Rodgers asks me. Absolutely everyone has folklore, she believes, and we see it in small ways every single day: “whether it’s the Christmas pudding recipe annotated by your great-grandma that you make every year, or pupils signing each other’s shirts at the end of the school term”.

A lot of us don’t realise we’re participating in folklore, says Parkes-Nield. “If you blow out candles on a birthday cake, if you take part in the ritualised behaviour involved in a stag or hen do, all of those things are folkloric”.

In essence, folklore is the practices, traditions and stories people share together. It encompasses crafts, dance, songs, tales, beliefs. And it usually has an element of received knowledge passed from one generation to the next, and that evolves by word of mouth rather than formalised means.

Folklore is sometimes best explained by what it’s not: not purely historical, not only the paranormal, not just middle-aged white men morris dancing around isolated villages where incomers face ritual immolation.

Indeed, morris dancing is a fine example of the more inclusive aspect of the folk revival: once exclusively male, there are now as many female dancers as men, with the growth of queer and feminist troupes like Boss Morris, who have performed with Wet Leg at the Brit Awards and Glastonbury.
Why are younger people so engaged in folklore?

Folklore can be very analogue, says Parkes-Nield. It’s tangible and, particularly in a post-pandemic world, a way to meet the people on your doorstep – whether it is learning a heritage craft like wheat-weaving, editing a fanzine or visiting local standing stones with other curious neighbours.

And, while folklore absolutely proliferates through digital means – look up WitchTok or #pagan on your social media of choice – it also offers a way of getting offline and meeting people across generations, in a time when so much entertainment is segregated and screen-based.

All of this has pretty obvious positive effects for mental health, as young people in particular struggle in an increasingly disconnected world. And it satisfies a craving for spiritual exploration that extends beyond organised religion – according to recent census data shamanism is the fastest growing belief system in the UK.

In her research, Parkes-Nield sees folklore societies popping up all over the shop – one such is Folk Club, based in south London and set up four years ago by Ellie Dempsey and Elizabeth Bailey. Now in her early 30s, Bailey grew up in the countryside, but didn’t really consider the folk rituals that were part of her childhood until she moved to the capital.

The escalating climate emergency is without doubt tied to the current resurgence, she thinks. “Folklore often sees a revival at points of national crisis, because it’s so much about coming together and connecting with the natural world.”

But, while Bailey also notes an appetite for learning about the seasonal traditions that were once passed down organically, the pull is not backwards. “A big part of the folk revival is that folk is by the people, for the people. That means re-examining some practices, making them more inclusive, and taking the opportunity to update traditions that have stagnated or been co-opted.”

She also draws a direct line between the political roots of folklore and this current iteration, like the Right to Roam protesters summoning Old Crockern, the mythical guardian spirit of Dartmoor, or Extinction Rebellion crowds banging pots and pans. “This is folklore being created.”

The folklore revival has been greeted with scepticism in some quarters, wary of the potential for co-option for a more nationalist or far-right agenda. The academics and practitioners I spoke to are well aware of how “Englishness” has become contentious in recent years, in particular the aggressive use of the St George’s flag by anti-immigrant activists.

But they argue these customs are far from nationalistic – many happen on a more hyperlocal scale than national. Folklore is often historically anti-establishment, and its practices at times suppressed with the same force and misogyny directed towards women accused of witchcraft. There are plenty of calendar customs, for example, cancelled by the establishment because of what was considered to be riotous behaviour by the lower classes. And many traditions were founded by communities wanting to celebrate themselves beyond the dominant culture: the Notting Hill carnival is perhaps the best-known example of this.

Academics talk about “multifolkloric Britain”, says Rodgers. “We can’t track where certain elements of folklore come from because we’ve always had people arriving and leaving, bringing and taking away things. So folklore is naturally diverse and inclusive.”
But the current revival is offering a moment of correction. She quotes the writer David Southwell, creator of the folkloric fantasy Hookland, who argues: “Re-enchantment is resistance”.

“Nvidia chief quits after claims of affairs with ‘spy’ and employee”, is the Guardian’s front page today, while the FT goes with “Huang exit plunges Nvidia into crisis”.
The Times leads on “Six women say they too were preyed on by Brand”, the Sun writes “Monster’s mansion”.

The i Paper has “Britain set for a new deal with the EU”, the Mail’s take is “Staggering cost of PM’s EU reset”, and the Express says “PM’ ‘obsessed with selling us out to the EU’”. The Telegraph says “Taxman to hound bereaved for decades”, the Mirror has “100 knives off our streets every day”, and Metro writes “Not so flush now”.
Why Democrat Scott Colom’s victory in Mississippi Senate race was so historic

Mississippi has elected the Democrat Scott Colom in a historic race in the traditionally deep-red state, making him its first Black senator since shortly after the US civil war. The closely contested race was called more than a week after the US midterms, with Colom running against the Republican incumbent, Cindy Hyde-Smith. How did Colom’s grassroots campaign win despite limited early backing from national Democrats? Lucy Hough speaks to politics and democracy reporter George Chidi.
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad
Datacentres are usually built without the consent of locals, consume vast amounts of electricity and water, and enrich rapacious tech companies.

But in Falun, Sweden, stands a datacentre with a difference. Made from wood, its electricity supply is 100% renewable, its back-up generators run on a fossil-free biofuel, and it pumps its excess heat into Falun’s local district heating system. These are just a few of its sustainable credentials.
Its creation was also initiated by government with local benefits built in, such as 60% of its capital expenditure being invested locally in areas such as education, training and youth activities.
Datacentres may be an inevitable part of our digital future, but Sweden’s approach shows there might be a kinder way to get there.
